name: Amazon S3
summary: AWS’s object storage, and the de facto API most object stores copy.
intro: Amazon S3 stores objects (files plus metadata) in buckets, addressed by a key such as `logs/2026/10/05/app.json`. You read and write whole objects over HTTPS, and S3 scales to any number of objects without you provisioning capacity.

Amazon S3 stores objects in buckets and is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability in every storage class. The choice you make for each object is its storage class, which trades storage price against access cost, how quickly the first byte comes back, and how many Availability Zones hold a copy. Choose well and the same data costs a fraction as much. Choose badly and retrieval fees or minimum storage durations eat the savings.
strengths: Designed for 11 nines of durability, with no capacity planning
Storage classes and lifecycle rules make cold data very cheap
Its API is the standard: MinIO, Cloudflare R2, Google Cloud Storage and most data tools speak it
limits: Objects are replaced whole; there’s no appending to or editing part of a file
Per-request fees add up for millions of tiny files
Data transfer out to the internet is billed, which can dominate costs for public downloads
A bucket isn’t a file system: “folders” are key prefixes, and renaming one copies every object under it. Mount it with S3 Files or Mountpoint when software needs files

snippet.title: Upload, list and fetch with the AWS CLI

sections.title: A bucket is not a disk
body: A disk (a physical SSD, or a block volume such as EBS) is just a long row of numbered blocks. It knows nothing about files. Ask it for block 81,920 and it returns 4 KB of bytes.

A file system such as ext4, NTFS or XFS is software that turns those blocks into named files inside folders. It tracks which blocks belong to which file, and gives you the operations programs expect: open a file, change bytes in the middle, append to the end, rename a folder in one step, lock a file, set permissions. A network file system (NFS or SMB, as in EFS) runs that software on a server and lets many machines mount the same folders.

An S3 bucket is neither. It is a flat map from keys to objects that you reach over HTTPS with a handful of calls: `PUT` a whole object, `GET` all or a byte range of one, `LIST` keys by prefix, `DELETE`. There is no file system inside it, so no operating system can mount it out of the box. The folders you see in the console are an illusion: the key `photos/2026/a.jpg` is one string that happens to contain slashes, and the console groups keys by the text before each `/`.

That difference is why “just put it on S3” sometimes fails: a program that opens a file and edits part of it, renames a temporary file into place, or takes a lock assumes a file system. To run it against a bucket, something has to translate file operations into S3 calls. That is what mounting S3 means.

sections.title: Disk, file system or bucket?
columns: File system (ext4 on a disk, or EFS)

rows.label: What it stores
values: Named files in nested folders, built on blocks

rows.label: How you reach it
values: Attached to a machine as a device, e.g. `/dev/nvme1n1`
HTTPS API calls from anywhere with permission

rows.label: Folders
values: None; it doesn’t know about files
None; keys containing `/` that tools display as folders

rows.label: Change bytes in the middle
values: No; upload the whole object again

rows.label: Append to the end
values: No (Express One Zone directory buckets can)

rows.label: Rename a folder
values: Copy and delete every object under the prefix

rows.label: Locks and permissions
values: No locks; access is set by IAM and bucket policies

rows.label: Who can use it at once
values: One machine (ext4) or many (EFS, over NFS)

rows.label: Typical latency
values: Under a millisecond to a few milliseconds
Under a millisecond locally; a few over NFS

notes: You never use a disk without a file system: formatting it with `mkfs` is the step that puts one on it. A bucket can’t be formatted, which is why mounting one needs a translator.

sections.title: What mounting a bucket does
sections.intro: Both apps read files from what looks like an ordinary folder. Underneath, each file operation becomes S3 requests.

diagram.caption: Mountpoint (top) turns every read into a GET to the bucket, so each one waits for S3. S3 Files (bottom) keeps recently used small files on its own fast storage, answers most reads there, and goes to the bucket only for the rest. Real S3 replies take tens of milliseconds; here they’re slowed down so you can see them.

sections.title: Ways to put a file system on top of S3
sections.intro: None of these changes the bucket itself. Each one runs a file system somewhere else and maps it onto objects. They differ in how much of a real file system you get, and where it runs.

items.name: Amazon S3 Files
items.text: A managed file system, built on EFS, linked to a bucket or prefix. EC2, Lambda, ECS and EKS mount it over NFS 4.1/4.2 and get edits, renames, locks and POSIX permissions. Hot small files live on fast storage; changes are written back to the bucket as new object versions.

items.name: Mountpoint for Amazon S3
items.text: A client you run on the machine (`mount-s3`). Fast for reading big files and writing new ones in one pass, but it deliberately doesn’t fake what S3 can’t do: no editing existing files, no renames (except on directory buckets), no locks or symlinks.

items.name: s3fs-fuse, rclone mount
items.text: Older general-purpose mounts that emulate more of a file system, for example by re-uploading a whole object when one byte changes. Convenient, but slow and surprising under heavy writes, and not safe for several writers.

items.name: JuiceFS
items.text: A full POSIX file system that keeps its metadata in a database (Redis, PostgreSQL, SQLite and others) and stores file contents as chunks in a bucket. Renames and locks are real, but the bucket holds JuiceFS chunks, not your files as readable objects.

items.name: S3 File Gateway
items.text: A Storage Gateway appliance in your data centre that serves NFS or SMB shares to local machines and stores each file as an object in S3, with a local cache.

items.name: FSx for Lustre
items.text: A high-performance parallel file system for training and simulation jobs. It can be linked to a bucket, presenting its objects as files and exporting results back.

items.name: Directory buckets
items.text: Not a mount, but the closest S3 gets to a file system on its own: real directories, appending to objects, and an atomic `RenameObject` call. Single Availability Zone only.

sections.title: What survives the translation
sections.intro: The two AWS options take opposite approaches. Mountpoint is a thin, fast translator that refuses operations S3 can’t do directly. S3 Files is a real file system that syncs to the bucket in the background.

rows.label: Read a file, or part of one
values: Yes; small hot files in about a millisecond

rows.label: Write a new file
values: Yes, written once from start to end

rows.label: Edit an existing file
values: No; only replace it whole, with `--allow-overwrite`
Yes; the bucket gets a new object version

rows.label: Append
values: Only on Express One Zone, with `--incremental-upload`

rows.label: Rename a file or folder
values: Yes; instant on the mount, copied object by object in the bucket

rows.label: `chmod`, `chown`, symlinks
values: No; permissions are fixed at mount time

rows.label: See the change in the bucket
values: After 60 seconds without writes to the file

rows.label: Runs where
values: Any Linux machine with AWS credentials
Inside a VPC: EC2, Lambda, ECS, EKS

notes: S3 Files requires versioning on the bucket. If a file changes in the bucket and on the mount at the same time, the bucket wins and your copy is moved to a lost-and-found folder.
Neither can read objects in Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive until they are restored.
Renaming a folder with millions of objects through any mount is slow and costs one copy and one delete request per object, because the bucket itself has no folders.

sections.title: Mount a bucket
sections.intro: Mountpoint runs on the machine; S3 Files is created once, then mounted like any NFS share.
source: # Mountpoint for Amazon S3: a client on this machine
# S3 Files: create a file system linked to the bucket, then mount it
echo hello > /mnt/s3files/notes/today.txt   # appears as notes/today.txt in the bucket

sections.title: Retrieval speed by class
sections.intro: Each colour is a request for an object stored in a different class.

diagram.caption: An app reads four objects, each in a different storage class. Standard, Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval all answer in milliseconds; the last two charge per GB retrieved. The fourth object is in Glacier Deep Archive, so a restore job has to bring it back first. Real Standard restores take up to 12 hours; here they’re compressed to seconds.

sections.title: Storage classes at a glance

rows.label: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
values: Milliseconds; opt-in archive tiers take minutes to hours
None; objects under 128 KB aren’t tiered
None, plus a small monthly fee per monitored object

rows.label: S3 Express One Zone
values: Latency-critical data next to your compute

rows.label: S3 Standard-IA
values: Data read about once a month that must come back instantly

rows.label: S3 One Zone-IA
values: Re-creatable data read about once a month

rows.label: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
values: Archives read about once a quarter, instantly

rows.label: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
values: Backups and archives read about once a year
Minutes to hours, after a restore
Per GB; bulk restores are free

rows.label: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
values: Retention for years, read less than once a year

notes: Every class is designed for 11 nines of durability. The One Zone classes keep data in a single Availability Zone, so losing that zone can lose the data.
Minimum duration: if you delete, overwrite or transition an object sooner, you’re still billed for the full period.
Minimum billed size: smaller objects are billed as 128 KB. The two Glacier archive classes add 40 KB of metadata per object: 32 KB billed at the archive rate and 8 KB at the Standard rate.
Express One Zone stores data in directory buckets and doesn’t support lifecycle transitions.

sections.title: Intelligent-Tiering, tier by tier
sections.intro: Intelligent-Tiering moves each object between tiers based on when it was last read, and moves it back to Frequent Access when it’s read again. There are no retrieval fees.

items.name: Frequent Access
items.text: Where new objects start. Millisecond access.

items.name: Infrequent Access
items.text: Objects nobody has read for 30 consecutive days. Still millisecond access, at a lower storage price.

items.name: Archive Instant Access
items.text: Objects nobody has read for 90 consecutive days. Still millisecond access, and cheaper again.

items.name: Archive Access
items.text: Optional, for data your application can wait for. Objects must be restored first, which takes minutes to hours.

items.name: Deep Archive Access
items.text: Optional. Restores finish within 12 hours, as with Glacier Deep Archive.

sections.title: Getting archived objects back
sections.intro: Objects in Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Glacier Deep Archive, or in Intelligent-Tiering’s opt-in archive tiers, can’t be read directly. You first call `RestoreObject`, which makes a temporary readable copy, and choose how fast that should happen.

rows.label: Glacier Flexible Retrieval, or the Archive Access tier
Glacier Deep Archive, or the Deep Archive Access tier

notes: Expedited times apply to objects under 250 MB, and Expedited requests may be turned away at busy times unless you buy provisioned capacity.
Standard retrievals are free for objects in Intelligent-Tiering.
Restore requests are limited to 1,000 per second per account. To restore millions of objects, use S3 Batch Operations.

items.name: Read often, or you don’t know
items.text: Start in S3 Standard. If access patterns are unknown or change over time, Intelligent-Tiering finds the savings for you without retrieval fees.

items.name: Read about once a month
items.text: Cheaper storage with a per-GB retrieval fee. Use One Zone-IA only for data you could re-create, such as replicas or derived files.

items.name: Read a few times a year, instantly
items.text: Medical images, news archives, uploads from years ago: rarely read, but when they are, someone is waiting.

items.name: Read rarely, can wait hours
items.text: Backups, compliance archives and raw data kept for years. Deep Archive is S3’s cheapest class and an alternative to tape.

items.name: Latency is the bottleneck
items.text: ML training, interactive analytics and other request-heavy jobs running in the same Availability Zone. AWS quotes up to 10x faster access than S3 Standard.

items.name: Lots of small objects
items.text: In the IA classes and Glacier Instant Retrieval, objects under 128 KB are billed as 128 KB, and Intelligent-Tiering doesn’t tier them. Bundle small files, or leave them in Standard.

sections.title: Automate it with a lifecycle rule
sections.intro: Lifecycle rules move objects to colder classes as they age and can delete them at the end. Save this as `lifecycle.json` and apply it with `aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket my-bucket --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json`.

items.name: Versioning
items.text: Keeps every version of an object, so an overwrite or delete can be undone. Pair it with a lifecycle rule that expires old versions.

items.name: Object Lock
items.text: Write once, read many: objects can’t be deleted or overwritten until a date you set. Used for compliance and ransomware protection.

items.name: Replication
items.text: Copies new objects to another bucket in the same or another Region, optionally into a cheaper storage class.

items.name: Strong consistency
items.text: Since December 2020, a read after a successful write or delete always sees the change, for every object in every Region.

items.name: Event notifications
items.text: Trigger a Lambda function, an SQS queue, an SNS topic or an EventBridge rule when objects are created or deleted.

items.name: S3 Tables
items.text: Table buckets that store Apache Iceberg tables and run compaction and snapshot clean-up for you, for a higher storage price plus per-object monitoring and compaction fees.

items.name: Very large objects
items.text: A single object can be up to 50 TB, raised from 5 TB in December 2025. Upload anything over about 100 MB in parallel parts with multipart upload.

sections.title: The same idea at other providers
sections.intro: Every major cloud offers hot-to-archive tiers. The names differ, and so do the details: Google’s Archive class is still readable in milliseconds, while Azure’s Archive tier must be rehydrated first.

rows.label: Yearly or less
values: Glacier Flexible Retrieval (90 days), Deep Archive (180 days)

rows.label: Automatic tiering
values: Lifecycle rules on last access time

values: S3 Files mount; directory buckets for real directories
Hierarchical namespace buckets; Cloud Storage FUSE to mount
Data Lake Storage hierarchical namespace; BlobFuse2 or NFS 3.0 to mount

story: In 2005 Amazon’s retail business had a storage problem of its own: product images, videos and other data that had to be kept cheaply and reliably at a scale that kept growing. Werner Vogels later wrote that “the majority of our data needed an object (or key-value) store”, and that the block and file storage on the market couldn’t offer low cost with high reliability.

AWS launched S3 on 14 March 2006 with a one-paragraph announcement. It stored objects of 1 byte to 5 GB under a key you chose, reached over REST or SOAP, for $0.15 per GB-month plus $0.20 per GB transferred, with no minimum fee. Behind it sat about 1 PB of capacity on roughly 400 storage nodes in 15 racks across three data centres. Its stated design principles were decentralization, asynchrony, autonomy and failure tolerance, so that no single machine could become a bottleneck or a single point of failure.

S3’s bucket-and-key HTTP API became the interface many other object stores copy. At its 20th birthday in March 2026 it held more than 500 trillion objects across hundreds of exabytes, served over 200 million requests a second and charged about 2 cents per GB. AWS says code written against it in 2006 still works unchanged.

choices.choice: A flat key-value store over HTTP, not a file system
choices.why: Most of Amazon’s own data was whole objects fetched by key. Leaving out directories, partial writes and locks let S3 spread data over many commodity machines and serve it to any program on the internet.

choices.choice: Cheap commodity hardware that expects failure
choices.why: Building from commodity parts kept costs low, so the system was designed around machines failing: every object is stored in several places and no single node is in charge.

Caches in S3’s metadata layer kept it highly available but meant a read could, rarely, return stale data. In December 2020 a cache coherence protocol made every read see the latest write, at no extra cost.

choices.choice: Pay per GB, with no minimum
choices.why: Billing only for what was stored and transferred meant a developer could start with one object and grow without buying capacity up front.
